title: Gyoza
subtitle: crisp-bottomed Japanese pan-fried dumplings
excerpt: Gyoza are Japanese pan-fried dumplings with a crisp base and steamed top. The filling is pork mince with shredded cabbage, ginger, and garlic. Making the wrappers from scratch takes time but the texture is far better than shop-bought.
sourceNotes: Gyoza are Japanese pan-fried dumplings adapted from Chinese jiaozi. They arrived in Japan after World War Two and quickly became a fixture of ramen shops and izakayas. The Japanese version is thinner-skinned than its Chinese counterpart and is almost always pan-fried then steamed.

content.text: The defining texture of gyoza is the contrast between the crisp, golden base and the soft, steamed top. This comes from the pan-fry-then-steam method. The dough for the wrappers is simple -- just flour and boiling water -- but needs 30 minutes to rest before rolling.

items.prepNote: for the wrappers -- mix with 100ml boiling water and knead into a smooth dough
finely shredded, then salted and squeezed dry

content.text: Make the dough: mix flour with 100ml boiling water. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Combine pork mince, squeezed cabbage, ginger, garlic, spring onion, and soy sauce in a bowl. Mix well.
Roll the dough into a long cylinder and cut into 20 to 24 pieces. Roll each piece into a thin circle about 9cm wide. Place a teaspoon of filling in the centre. Fold and pleat the edges to seal.
Heat oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat. Place the gyoza flat-side down in a single layer. Fry for 2 minutes until the bottoms are golden.
Add 80ml of water to the pan. Immediately cover with a lid. Steam for 5 to 6 minutes until the water has evaporated and the filling is cooked through.
Remove the lid and cook for 1 more minute to crisp the bases. Serve with a dipping sauce of soy sauce and rice vinegar.

items.symptom: Gyoza stick to the pan and tear when lifted
items.cause: Not enough oil or pan not hot enough before adding the dumplings
items.fix: Make sure the oil is shimmering before adding the gyoza. Do not move them until the bottoms are properly golden. A non-stick pan helps.

content.text: Gyoza are found at virtually every ramen shop and izakaya in Japan. The combination of crisp bottom and steamed top is the defining texture. They are usually served with a small bowl of soy sauce and rice vinegar for dipping. Making wrappers from scratch takes time but the texture is worth it.
